Guide

Essential Oil Dilution Chart

Last updated 26 October 2026

What the percentages mean, how many drops that actually is, and the oils in our range that need a lower ceiling than usual.

Nearly every problem people have with essential oils is a dosing problem. Not the wrong oil, not a fake oil — simply too much of it. This page is the reference we point people to.

What a percentage means

Dilution is the proportion of essential oil to carrier oil by volume. You do not need to measure precisely, because there is a shortcut worth memorising: one drop in one teaspoon (5 ml) of carrier is roughly 1%.

DilutionPer teaspoon (5 ml)Per 30 mlTypical use
0.5%half a drop3 dropsClove, cinnamon, thyme — anything flagged as a sensitiser
1%1 drop6 dropsThe face, sensitive skin, and most blends for older children
2%2 drops12 dropsGeneral body use — the everyday default
3%3 drops18 dropsShort-term, on a small area

Half a drop is not a practical measurement. For anything needing 0.5% or less, make up 30 ml at a time rather than trying to split drops.

Oils that need a lower ceiling

Most oils are comfortable at 2% on the body. These are the ones in our range that are not, with the limit for each. Every figure here is the same one printed on that oil's own page.

OilMaximum on skinWhy
Clove Bud 0.5% A strong skin sensitiser. Keep to 0.5% or below on skin, avoid in pregnancy, and keep well away from children and pets.
Thyme 0.5% A strong skin irritant and sensitiser. Keep to 0.5% or below, avoid during pregnancy, and avoid entirely if you have high blood pressure. Not for children.
Cinnamon Leaf 0.6% A skin sensitiser. Keep to 0.6% or below on skin and avoid during pregnancy.
Citronella 1% A known skin sensitiser — keep to 1% or below, and avoid during pregnancy.
Lemongrass 1% More irritating to skin than its freshness suggests — keep to 1% or below.
Sweet Fennel 1% High in trans-anethole. Avoid during pregnancy and while breastfeeding, avoid with oestrogen-sensitive conditions, and keep away from children. Keep to 1% on skin.
Tea Tree Shield 1% Genuinely toxic to cats and dogs, including as vapour in a closed room. Dilute to 1% or below on skin; never apply it neat.
Sweet Basil 1.5% Avoid during pregnancy, and keep to 1.5% or below on skin.

Diffusing is a different question

Percentages apply to skin. In a diffuser the guidance is simpler: four to six drops scents an ordinary room, and more does not scent it better. Past about six drops most people stop registering the increase at all.

Olfactory fatigue sets in within minutes — your nose stops reporting a smell that has not changed — which is exactly when people add more. The person who walks in half an hour later gets the full force of it.

Four things people get wrong

  1. Applying neat. "It is natural, so it is gentle" is the most expensive assumption in this hobby. Neat application is how most people develop a permanent sensitivity, and sensitisation does not wear off.
  2. Treating every oil the same. Lavender at 2% is unremarkable. Clove at 2% is a problem. The dilution depends on the oil, not the task.
  3. Scaling a blend by eye. Doubling a recipe means doubling the carrier too. People routinely double the essential oil and leave the carrier where it was.
  4. Using an old bottle. Oxidised oils irritate more than fresh ones at the same dilution — citrus and tea tree especially.

Start lower than you think

There is no prize for using more. A 1% blend you can wear daily is worth more than a 4% blend that leaves you itchy and wary of the whole thing. If you are unsure, start at 1%, patch-test on the inside of your forearm, and wait 24 hours.
